extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of epic literature / mythology (readers of the Mahabharata translation)
extracted.subtask_description: A prose translation excerpt from the Mahabharata narrating the gambling match, exile, and moral debates; contains narrative norms and social/moral expectations embedded in the story. Useful for analysis of epic narrative, ethical norms, and traditional social rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness of gambling (moral requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deceitful gambling is sinful, and unworthy a Kshatriya; wise men do not applaud a player who winneth by foul means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly condemns trickery in play: a gambler must not use deceit; winning by foul means is dishonourable. This is presented as a moral standard for behaviour in contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit promise of fair play before contest
rubrics_metrics.description: "I will play if mine opponent will promise to throw fairly, without trickery and deceit. Deceitful gambling is sinful..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A challenger/contestant should require and obtain an explicit assurance of honest play before participating; absence of such a promise delegitimises the match in participants' view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional practice: same person should throw and stake
rubrics_metrics.description: Yudhishthira objects that 'One man is to throw the dice and another is to lay the stakes. Such is contrary to all practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The accepted convention is that the player and the stake-laying party should correspond; separation of the thrower and the staker is improper and signals likely foul play (as in Shakuni/Duryodhana's arrangement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of stakes between opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Yudhishthira asks 'first say who doth challenge and who is to lay stakes equally with me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakes should be laid equally by/for both sides; asymmetric arrangements undermine legitimacy and fairness of the contest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of wagering another's person when they lack autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Vidura points out that Yudhishthira 'hast staked his own self, for now thou hast become a slave; but if thou wilt stake Draupadi now and win, all that thou hast lost will be restored unto thee.' And later: 'Thou couldst not win aught from a slave who had no power to stake the princess.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One may not lawfully stake or transfer ownership of a person who does not possess the autonomy to be wagered (e.g., someone already rendered a slave or when the wagerer no longer has authority to stake another). This is used to argue the illegitimacy of Draupadi's being staked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of a Kshatriya to accept challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Yudhishthira: 'I cannot refuse the invitation of Dhritarashtra, or, like a true Kshatriya, disdain a challenge either to fight or to play with his peers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social ideal: a warrior (Kshatriya) should not refuse legitimate challenges to combat or contest from his peers; refusal may be seen as dishonourable. This functions as a cultural norm constraining refusal even when risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Husband's/kshatriya's duty to protect wife and family honour
rubrics_metrics.description: Draupadi reproaches her husbands: 'Is it not the duty of a husband to protect his wife?... These husbands of mine, who have the prowess of lions, saw me afflicted, nor lifted a hand to save.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a normative expectation that husbands, especially warriors, must protect the honour and safety of their wives; failure to do so is censured and used as moral indictment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctity of a woman's hair and modest dress
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A woman's hair is sacred.' 'Can a modest woman appear before strangers in loose attire?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats a woman's hair (especially when sanctified) as sacred and requires modest dress in public; forcibly exposing or handling a woman's hair is presented as a grave violation and sacrilege.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemnation of dishonesty as path to ruin
rubrics_metrics.description: Vidura: 'Thy words are wicked, O Duryodhana... Thy practis(ing) dishonesty will accomplish yet the ruin of the Kauravas.' 'Dishonesty is one of the doors to hell.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dishonest behaviour—particularly in rulers—invites divine/human retribution and eventual ruin. Presented as practical moral guidance and forewarning, supported by omens and prophetic remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue of forgiveness and self-control (ethical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Yudhishthira argues: 'Anger is sinful; it is the cause of destruction... The wise man who learns how to forgive attaineth to Brahma... Forgiveness, O beautiful one! is holiness; it is Truth; it is Brahma.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-control and forgiveness are elevated as supreme virtues, superior to immediate vengeance. Controlling wrath is associated with wisdom, spiritual attainment, and good governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to act (kshatriya valor) versus restraint—timeliness of retaliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrasting voices: Draupadi and Bhima urge action and vengeance—'The hour hath now come for thee to seek vengeance; the present is not a time for forgiveness.' Bhima: 'If I am not permitted to punish the tormentor of Draupadi, bring me a fire...'—while Yudhishthira defends restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative sets up a tension: while forgiveness/self-control is ideal, there is also an expectation that warriors should take timely, forceful action to redress gross wrongs. The 'right moment' for Kshatriya action is an important normative criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of omens as portents requiring heed
rubrics_metrics.description: After the outrage, 'a jackal howled in the sacrificial chamber. Asses brayed... those who heard these dread omens exclaimed: "Swashti!" Dhritarashtra shook with terror.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strange or inauspicious omens are to be taken seriously as signals of divine displeasure or impending doom; appropriate reaction includes prayer, repentance, and seeking to avert wrath through expiation or counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of wager terms and consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: For the second match the Kauravas arrange: 'the side which loseth shall go into exile for twelve full years, and into concealment for a year thereafter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contests involving large stakes must define explicit, agreed-upon terms (duration of exile, penalties). Ambiguity or clandestine methods (loaded dice) subvert fairness and lead to grave consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oaths and vows as binding moral commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Bhima's vow: 'May I never reach Heaven if I do not yet seize Duhsasana in battle and, tearing open his breast, drink his very life blood!...' Draupadi's vow about her hair until Bhima slays Duhsasana.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public, solemn vows commit actors to future courses of vengeance or reparation; such vows function as social and moral constraints motivating future action and are treated as serious promises with cosmic implications.
